hints: Focus on the three $\text{-OH}$ groups only and for each one count how many other carbon atoms are directly attached to the carbon bearing the $\text{-OH}$.
walkthrough:
Classify by the carbon carrying the OH**
Remember you never classify by the oxygen, you classify by the carbon it is stuck to. If that carbon is attached to 1 other carbon it is primary, to 2 other carbons it is secondary, to 3 other carbons it is tertiary. Scan calcitriol and you will find exactly three $\text{-OH}$ groups.

Sort the three groups**
The two $\text{-OH}$ groups on the bottom six membered ring are each on a $\text{CH}$ inside the ring, bonded to two ring carbons, so both are secondary. The $\text{-OH}$ on the top right side chain is on a carbon bonded to three alkyl carbons, $\text{C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$, so it is tertiary. There is no $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ group, so primary is 0.
Final answer: primary 0 secondary 2 tertiary 1

hints: Look for carbon atoms with four different groups, remembering that in rings two directions around the ring count as different groups and $\text{C=C}$ carbons can never be chiral.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
A chiral carbon has four single bonds to four different groups. Immediately rule out all $\text{C=C}$ carbons, all $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons, all $\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ carbons and the quaternary ring junction bearing two ring $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups that are identical at the first point of difference in some cases. You are left with $\text{CH}$ and $\text{CR}_{4}$ centres to check carefully.

Count across the molecule**
You find two on the lower diol ring, both $\text{CH(OH)}$, plus four in the upper steroid fragment and side chain: the ring junction carbons and the two side chain carbons bearing $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}$. The total is 6.
Final answer: 6 chiral carbon atoms

hints: Count only $\text{C=C}$ bonds where each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups, the terminal $\text{C=CH}_{2}$ cannot show geometrical isomerism.
walkthrough:
Find which double bonds can twist into isomers**
Picture each $\text{C=C}$. For $E/Z$ isomerism each end must have two different substituents. Calcitriol has three $\text{C=C}$ bonds in the triene system. The exocyclic $\text{C=CH}_{2}$ on the lower ring has two $\text{H}$ atoms on one end, so it cannot show geometrical isomerism. The other two $\text{C=C}$ bonds, the central $\text{-CH=CH-}$ and the exocyclic bond joining the upper ring to the chain, both have two different groups at each end.

Use the 2 to the power n rule**
With $n = 2$ independent $E/Z$ centres, the maximum number of stereoisomers is $$2^{n} = 2^{2} = 4$$ including calcitriol itself.
Final answer: 4 geometrical isomers

hints: Draw X and look for a plane of symmetry that makes some $\text{C=O}$ carbons and the $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons equivalent to each other.
walkthrough:
Map symmetry in X**
X is a cyclic tetraketone, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{4}$, with four $\text{C=O}$ carbons and two $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons. It is highly symmetrical. The two $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons are equivalent to each other, while the four $\text{C=O}$ carbons fall into three different environments. That gives $1 + 3 = 4$ distinct carbon environments, so 4 peaks in the $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum.

hints: Recall the two very different shift regions for saturated alkyl carbons and for carbonyl carbons.
Think about which type of carbon in X is alkyl ($\text{CH}_{2}$ next to $\text{C=O}$) and which type is carbonyl ($\text{C=O}$).
Use your peak count from (i) to split the total of 4 peaks between the alkyl region and the carbonyl region.
walkthrough:
Separate alkyl from carbonyl**
In $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR, $\text{sp}^{3}$ alkyl carbons appear upfield, typically $\delta$ 0 to 50, even when next to a carbonyl. Ketone $\text{C=O}$ carbons are strongly deshielded and appear far downfield, typically $\delta$ 190 to 220.

Assign the counts**
X has only these two types. The two equivalent $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons give just one peak in the $\delta$ 25-50 range. The four ketone carbons in three environments give three peaks in the $\delta$ 190-220 range. That accounts for all 4 peaks predicted in (i).

Final answer: $\delta$ 25-50 ppm: 1 peak for $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons.
$\delta$ 190-220 ppm: 3 peaks for $\text{C=O}$ ketone carbons.

hints: Count only hydrogens in X and ask whether the $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups are equivalent by symmetry.
walkthrough:
Look for protons only**
X contains no $\text{-OH}$ and no $\text{=CH-}$. The only protons are on the two $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups flanked by $\text{C=O}$ groups. By the symmetry of the molecule these four protons are all in the same chemical environment, so they give a single peak in the $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR spectrum.
Final answer: 1 peak

hints: Recall the n+1 rule where n is the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atoms.
Check what atoms sit next to the $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups in X, are they $\text{CH}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$ or $\text{C=O}$ with no protons?
walkthrough:
Apply the n+1 rule**
Splitting is caused only by protons on the immediately neighbouring carbons. If there are $n$ such neighbouring protons, the signal splits into $n+1$ lines.

See zero neighbours**
Each $\text{CH}_{2}$ in X is sandwiched between two $\text{C=O}$ carbons. Those carbonyl carbons carry no hydrogen atoms, so $n = 0$. Therefore $n+1 = 1$, a singlet with no splitting.
Final answer: singlet, as the adjacent carbon atoms are $\text{C=O}$ carbons with no protons / H atoms to couple with.

hints: Remember hot, concentrated, acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ cleaves every $\text{C=C}$ completely, it does not stop at the diol.
Ask what happens to a terminal $\text{=CH}_{2}$ fragment after cleavage, first to methanoic acid and then under vigorous oxidation.
walkthrough:
Picture vigorous cleavage**
Cold dilute $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ gives a diol, but hot concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ cuts the $\text{C=C}$ bond apart entirely. Each alkene carbon ends up as $\text{C=O}$: $\text{=CH}_{2}$ becomes $\text{HCHO}$ then $\text{HCOOH}$, $\text{=CH-}$ becomes $\text{HCOOH}$, $\text{=CR-}$ becomes a ketone, $\text{=CR}_{2}$ becomes a ketone.

Push the smallest fragment all the way**
The exocyclic methylene $\text{C=CH}_{2}$ on the lower ring therefore releases a one carbon fragment. Under excess hot oxidiser, methanoic acid $\text{HCOOH}$ is further oxidised to $\text{CO}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. That is the smallest carbon containing product.
Final answer: $\text{CO}_{2}$ formed by oxidative cleavage of the $\text{C=C}$ bonds, the terminal $\text{=CH}_{2}$ carbon is oxidised via $\text{HCOOH}$ with further oxidation to $\text{CO}_{2}$.

hints: The large fragment keeps the intact fused 6 and 5 membered rings plus the full side chain, with the cleavage point becoming a ketone and the tertiary alcohol unchanged.
walkthrough:
Build the large fragment logically**
Cut calcitriol at the exocyclic $\text{C=C}$ that joins the upper bicyclic part to the chain leading to X. The upper part keeps its fused 6 membered and 5 membered rings and the whole $\text{-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ side chain. Hot $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ converts the alkene carbon on this side into a ketone $\text{C=O}$ on the six membered ring.

Leave what cannot oxidise**
Secondary alcohols elsewhere would oxidise, but this large fragment has no secondary alcohol. Its only $\text{-OH}$ is tertiary, $\text{C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$, which has no $\text{C-H}$ to break and so resists oxidation and appears unchanged in the product.

Final answer: Skeletal formula of bicyclic keto alcohol: fused 6-membered ring with $\text{C=O}$ at the cleavage position joined to 5-membered ring bearing side chain $\text{-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ where the tertiary alcohol is unchanged.
